items.body:
Airbrushed, subtropical, new age ambient-jazz from Jesse Peterson’s Maui-based project, given its highest profile platform to date on Amsterdam’s Music From Memory, and warmly advised to admirers of his regular spars, Carlos Niño, Laraaji, Mia Doi Todd...

"Originally formed in New York in the late 2000s, Turn On The Sunlight has evolved into a fluid, location-spanning practice rooted in collaboration, intuition and process. Now based on Maui, Peterson’s work draws together a wide network of musicians and environments, with recordings taking shape across Los Angeles, Tokyo, London, San Miguel de Allende and Haʻikū.

Loosely situated within a framework of organic, ambient-leaning jazz, 'Iseo' unfolds as a series of open, exploratory pieces, with electronics sitting subtly beneath acoustic and environmental elements. Built from layered instrumentation including synthesizers, guitar, zither, flutes, voice and field recordings, Peterson moves between grounded, tactile detail and more expansive, immersive states. A sense of warmth and permeability runs throughout: organic percussion, environmental textures and drifting rhythmic elements lend the record a gently saturated humidity, reflecting Peterson’s base in Hawaii, where the presence of nature is felt as much as it is heard.

Underlying the project is a way of working rooted in gathering, listening and tending. Instruments, ensemble sessions, field recordings and everyday environments are approached with attentiveness, shaped through collecting, refining and allowing things to settle. Relationships, landscape and lived experience shape the sound, giving 'Iseo' a tactile, almost hand-made quality.

Rather than fixed arrangements, the album feels as if it has been organically and lovingly assembled through a process of listening and response, each element finding its place within a wider, evolving whole. This approach reaches a natural centre point in the 15-minute piece 'Medianoche En La Calle Aurora', which unfolds patiently, bending through shifting environments as motifs and textures emerge and dissolve with quiet continuity.

Peterson’s role as both instigator and facilitator is central to the project. Bringing together a diverse group of collaborators including Carlos Niño, Mia Doi Todd, Laraaji, Ko Ishikawa, Luis Pérez Ixoneztli and Miles Spilsbury, he creates space for individual voices to emerge within a shared language. The result is a music defined by openness and generosity.

'Iseo' takes its title from Peterson’s son’s middle name, a word that can be understood to mean ‘one-world life’. The piece itself takes the form of a gentle lullaby, its melody loosely shaped around the syllables of his name and sung to Peterson’s son by Luis Pérez Ixoneztli, a close collaborator whose presence across the record reflects a long-standing relationship that extends beyond the music itself.

Sleeve art and design by Michael Willis."

items.body:
Inspired by Ennio Morricone, J.J. Cale and Hindustani classical music, Michael Brook's 1992 4AD debut is a 2nd wave ambient/new age classic, finally remastered and bundled with the genius follow-up EP 'Live at the Aquarium'. Unmissable FFO Jon Hassell, Harold Budd, Daniel Lanois, Brian Eno and David Sylvian.

Brook is best known for his soundtrack work at this point - his influential scores for films like 'An Inconvenient Truth' and 'The Fighter' - but rewind back to the early 1990s and he was living in London, jobbing as a producer and working with Brian Eno. He'd released a few records by that point, collaborating with Eno and Daniel Lanois on his Editions EG debut 'Hybrid' and collaborating with Dutch artist Pieter Nooten on the excellent 'Sleeps with the Fishes' in 1987. But his most important contribution had arguably been his Infinite Guitar, a modified electric guitar that allowed him to play long sitar-like drones. He used that technique on Jon Hassell's beloved 1986 album 'Power Spot' and famously built an instrument for the Edge, who played it on 'With or Without You'. And while he was working with other musicians, he was sketching out ideas for this next record, working slowly in his bedsit in-between commercial work and attempting to adapt the music he loved, particularly bluegrass and the work of Indian flute player Pannalal Ghosh.

Unsurprisingly, it's Brook's guitar sounds that take the lead from the beginning, muddled with woozy synths and assistance from a team of his close associates: Brian Eno, Daniel Lanois, Roger Eno, Dead Can Dance's James Pinker, violinist Hahn Rowe, Hassell collaborator Richard Henderson and viola player Nell Catchpole. The music is very much of its era, a core text for 4AD or Les Disques Du Crepusule heads, and illustrates just how quickly "ambient" and "new age" music were evolving. Brook hadn't been classically trained, so was urged by Hassell to do some lessons with La Monte Young, an experience that had led him to the Infinite Guitar in the first place. But long sustain wasn't the beginning and end of his interest in Hindustani classical music or in 20th century minimalism. You can hear just how the genres were being re-codified here, how traditional rhythms were being re-interpreted on drum machines and how Steve Reich's and Philip Glass's innovations were being absorbed by wide-eyed onlooker long before they became rave's after-hours staples.

If the album sounds a little frilly 35 years after its original release, that's mostly because Brook's sound was jumped on by Hollywood remarkably quickly. Just three years after 'Cobalt Blue' was released, the track 'Ultramarine' was conspicuously placed in Michael Mann's 'Heat' alongside selections from Terje Rydpal, Lisa Gerrard and Brian Eno. And he quickly became a staple, contributing to Hans Zimmer soundtracks like 'Mission: Impossible 2' and 'Black Hawk Down' and working on prestige projects like 'Into the Wild' and 'Brooklyn'. So if you're interested in hearing a more stripped down version of the album, then 4AD handily bundled it with 'Live at the Aquarium ' when they reissued the album for the first time in 1999. The show was recorded at the press party for the release of 'Cobalt Blue' and features Brook on his own, playing even more passionately and demonstrating the nuance of his signature technique.

items.body:
Memotone’s sublime, world-building ambient-jazz-fusion project yields a total gem for Accidental Meetings, perfused with the presence of Ugné Uma, Typesun & Jabu on a new highlight of his personalised microcosm, tipped for anyone on the line from Savath & Savalas to Moritz Von Oswald Trio, The Necks to Laurel Halo.

Active since 2011, it’s been a real pleasure to hear Will Yates cultivate his memotone sound into something more complex, yet not necessarily more complicated, on a slew of LPs for the likes of TTT, Sähkö, and World of Echo, plus that ace cut on Carrier’s debut LP. Club music is now long in the rearview, while ambient and jazz musics have taken precedence as the multi-instrumentalist continues to diversify his creative binds across more free-formed, expressive soundscapes, breezing with elements of spiritual jazz as much as psych folk, post rock,contemporary classical and strands of electronic music. 

‘Warm Shadows’ features some of his most seductive and expansive work, shaped with an underlying grasp of abstract, instrumental narratives that have become his calling card during this last decade. Intimacy and slowness are key to his exquisitely hushed appeal; unfolding the softest brushstrokes with patient electroacoustic nuance and attention to detail on two standouts with emergent Lithuanian vocalist Ugné Uma, who channels a mix of smouldering spiritual jazz and Eastern European melancholy on ‘Laimèti Pavyksta’, and even Sade-esque soul on the dusky closer ‘You Are Different.’ 

Elsewhere, the Bristolian connection makes for another highlight with Jabu’s Jasmine Butt’s subtle contribution to ‘Round The Bend,’ comparable to something from BoC’s ‘Campfire Headphase’, but left to his own devices memotone proves a consummate, atmospheric storyteller. Opener ‘For The Feral’ feels like a miniature of The Necks, and his feel for dreamy electro-acoustic texture best comes into play on ‘One Winged Bird’ and the tongue-tip moisture in the air of ‘The Freedom,’ all pointing to an artist arguably in their imperial phase. 

Tip!

items.body:
Abstract dub dream-weavers SKRS INTL. & WZRDRY remerge at the behest of Bristol’s Accidental Meetings for a super lush dose of wormholing ambient dance pressure tipped FFO Rezzett, Peak Oil/False Aralia, Second Woman.

‘Orbit Flares’ combines the two Canadian units for the first time in over a decade, naturally reprising an empathic level of vibes in a half hour of music that betrays illusive tekkerz developed over the interim. Any semblance of sharp edges are smudged to a brilliantly psychedelic, polychromatic lustre and laced with disciplined, yet properly wayward rhythms that tumble, buckle and vaporise in fractious delirium. Each new SKRS drop is welcome around ours but, jeez, they really push into their most impressive work here, possibly thanks to wzrdryAV’s synaesthetic suss.

Front to back it feel likes they catch minds/bodies in the split second before going under anaesthesia, and extrude us into pitch-bent helical vortices of plonging dub chords and gooey bass, finding bold new realms of computerised dub suss. Handrails are slippery as fuck, ground melts beneath feet, leaving bodies gyring in space between the weightless dub techno inflections of ‘1.1’, into air-stepping chicanery on ‘1.2’, or glitching like a hair-kissing Vladislav Delay on ‘1.3’. The smeared chords and scudding subs of ‘2.1’ call to mind Second Woman emulating the illusive dub-soul of False Aralia drops, and ‘2.3’ feels like distant rig heard on a Nitrous-induced permo. 

Sheer class for harder to please future dub freaks.

items.body:
Bay Area rapper Sha Ray teams up with DJ Haram on her debut album, spitting bold, unapologetic sex raps over Haram's heady but hard-hitting industrial-tinged beats. Heavy duty material FFO Gangsta Boo, Debby Friday or BbyMutha.

Back in 2022, Haram caught Sha Ray on stage in Brooklyn and was immediately struck by her presence. When Sha Ray tapped her for beats later on, she was already sold, meeting again face-to-face at an Armand Hammer/DJ Haram show in Los Angeles not long afterwards. But the collaboration didn't happen in a single studio; 'Critical Thot' is the result of a lengthy period of back-and-forth between Haram in Brooklyn and Sha Ray, who would reply to Haram's beats with demo versions of tracks and notes. As these demos evolved into proper tracks, Haram and Sha Ray's relationship blossomed and 'Critical Thot' emerged - a record that's inspired by both artists' experiences of their role as women in the music industry. 

Haram's grown significantly as a producer in the last few years. Her solo debut 'Beside Myself' was clearly a milestone, but she's also been spotted providing beats for a slew of Backwoodz regulars, from billy woods and Elucid to Ghais Guevara and Fielded. And 'Critical Thot' offers her the scratchpad she needed to try out some of her most adventurous ideas. Sha Ray doesn't stutter on 'The Material' when Haram cuts strings to ribbons over stuttering voices, oscillating from fast to slow, and although she meets Haram's snakelike Memphis groove with similar energy on 'Champagne and Bouquets', she's impressively unfazed when Haram pivots at the midway point, adding fairyale strings and musicbox chimes. 

Oakland rapper Nappy Nina shows up on 'Hey Queen' alongside Brookyln's JWords and both join Sha Ray for an alien-voiced deadpan over one of Haram's most uncompromising beats, a squashed, industrial-tinged speedrun through techno's muckiest edges that'd give Brodinski a run for his money. On 'Strictly', meanwhile, Haram pushes up the tempo to a brisk Jersey bounce and Sha Ray's charisma spills from every rubbery kick. "This is for my bitches, strictly for the bitches," she hisses. There's no doubt.

items.body:
Hamburg’s post-punk goth wraiths play the hits for John Peel, slinging cuts sifted from their four sessions recorded 1982-1985, including tearing renditions of ‘Incubus Succubus’ and ‘Qual’, a thunderous ‘Sehnsucht’, the very Cocteaus-esque ‘Polarlicht’, and tortured romance of ‘Autumn’

"You only need listen to the soul-devouring nocturnal visitation of Incubus Succubus, or the obliterating fury of Qual (“Meine Wiege ist deine Grab” – “my cradle is your grave”) to see that underestimating Xmal Deutschland was never a good idea. When the Hamburg band first walked into the BBC’s Maida Vale Studio in November 1982 to record their debut session for John Peel, it was natural they should feel a flash of awe as they were ushered through the labyrinthine building, on the brink of joining a radio lineage that included The Fall, David Bowie, Siouxsie And The Banshees and The Cure. Yet the band – at that point singer Anja Huwe, keyboardist Fiona Sangster, guitarist Manuela Rickers, drummer Manuela Zwingmann and bassist Wolfgang Ellerbrock – also quickly picked up on the old-school energy and hierarchies of the place, the entrenched divisions between tea ladies and the producers and sound engineers, the tensions between the old-school male rock’n’roll way of doing things and their band’s place in the modern world.

John Peel rarely came to the studio to meet the bands he had selected for the honour of a Peel Session, having no interest in pressing the showbiz flesh (For Lulu or otherwise). Instead, as Sangster recalls, Xmal Deutschland immediately found themselves up against producers and engineers who, regardless of the blessing inherent in Peel’s invitation, weren’t terribly impressed with the sight of this female-majority German band. “They communicated quite clearly that they didn’t think you were very good, that they didn’t like the music, and would you please hurry up,” says Sangster, bristling at the memory 43 years later.

Yet Xmal Deutschland had – in the jaded language of the old-fashioned male-dominated music industry – very much paid their dues by the time they arrived at Maida Vale. They formed in Hamburg in 1980 – “a tough city,” says singer Anja Huwe, a significantly grittier place than the artier musical enclaves of Cologne or Dusseldorf. They had endured – and thrived – in their canal-side rehearsal studio, against all the health-and-safety odds. The punks next-door had soundproofed their space with egg boxes; when somebody dropped a cigarette, the solvent went up in flames. “All dirty carpets and grotty sofas,” recalls Sangster. “It was filthy, it was damp, it was cold.” Zwingmann, meanwhile, recalls the dangerous swerving of their VW van as they raced for late-night ferries, burdened with equipment.

They had shown their own grit, too, by making the decision early on that they were not going to be channelled into the Neue Deutsche Welle, then a buzzword for young German bands. “If we’d stayed in Hamburg and gone down that path, our career would have been over in a year,” explains Huwe. “Because it was a very short-lived movement.” After releasing their first two singles on Hamburg imprint ZickZack, in 1983 they found the label that could match their questing, independent energy. “We recorded a tape in the rehearsal room and we took it to 4AD,” recalls Sangster. “We didn’t go anywhere else.” Fetish, their debut album for the label, followed. Like formidable, backcombed Groucho Marxes, they never wanted to belong to any club that would want them as a member. “We just didn’t want to give them the obvious sort of thing, and we always kept our distance from everyone,” says Huwe. “We were like a group on our own. We never went to a place like the Batcave – and they always invited us. Everyone wanted us to join, but we never went there because we were not interested. We went to exhibitions, we wrote books, saw films – you know, enjoyed our own company.”

This record, a fabulous chronological document of the four Peel sessions they recorded between November 1982 (five months before the release of their 1983 debut album Fetisch) and May 1985, is the sound of a band who knew the power of that company and who ultimately refused to be intimidated by the gruffly condescending gatekeepers of Maida Vale. They found a strength in defying their old-school attitudes. “We benefited from that because we sort of got into ‘fuck you’ mode”, says Sangster, much to Huwe and Zwingmann’s delight. “That might be part of the energy that you’re hearing.”

It’s an energy that transmits with a piercing clarity in these sixteen tracks, the constraints of time and space giving what Sangster calls “a certain urgency” to these sessions. “Listening back, you can tell it’s sort of like a hybrid between a live performance and a studio performance,” she says. “These are different versions, which is what makes them interesting.”

As Huwe and Sangster stress, a Peel session wasn’t the time for Xmal Deutschland to experiment – “you would choose one of the bangers!” they laugh. That’s clear from the opening full-pelt Incubus Succubus, its supernatural vortex immediately transporting the listener right into the room, to the dreamy expanses of closing track Autumn (from May 1985), their first song in English. In between arcs the remarkable career of a band in constant motion: “It’s a really interesting snapshot, as it were, of our evolution, these four Peel Sessions all together,” says Sangster. “You can see how we grew as a band.” It’s there in untethered experimentalism and proto-Mandinka howls of Reigen, from their second album Tocsin, or the new expansiveness that comes with Nachtschatten’s twinkling synths (not a million miles away from The Cure’s pop experiments) or the gorgeous melody of Der Wind. Here are the fierce hexes of their early work – the angel-devil showdown of Geheimnis, Qual’s scything B-side Sehnsucht, the tribal skitter of In Motion – mutating into a different kind of spellbinding. The studio atmosphere might have been oppressive, but this collection of Peel Sessions shows a band making the space their own. “It was so different compared to how we lived, because it was British, very conservative,” says Huwe. “But we jumped in there.” With this compilation, you can hear the ripples Xmal Deutschland made then still powerfully resonating down the years."

items.body: Anyone who has experienced someone close, and especially a young one, who was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, would be familiar with the existential and emotional rollercoaster that awaits all around those ill ones, along with the grief-filled, compassionate yet helpless years to come. Danish keyboard player and composer Anders Filipsen, the leader of the local experimental, electroacoustic ensemble The Black Nothing, experienced Alzheimer’s disease when his father was diagnosed four years ago. He composed a ten-part suite, Midt i en Fremtid (In the Middle of a Future), about the time he spent with his father, which composed passages, free improvisation, and graphic scores. He says: “This album is the sound of a time when what once was ceased to be, and something new emerged. It is a loving song to the moments we share now – in the midst of all that has disappeared”. The different parts of the suite function as tableaux of moments marked by gradual decline, filled with silence, relating to the inevitable time when the ill ones can not share their thoughts anymore, repetition, and intensity- a landscape where presence and memory meet in sound. The ten musicians - vocalist Qarin Wikström (who sings in Danish, but the lyrics were translated to English), trumpeter Emil Jensen, clarinetists Carolyn Goodwyn and Jeppe Højgaard (who also plays the flute), cellist Soma Allpas, double bass player and cellist Nils Bo Davidsen, electronics player Mads Emil Nielsen, percussionist Victor Dybbroe, drummer Bjørn Heebøl, and Filipsen on synths - use their idiosyncratic voices to create a unified expression in which individual playing and collective sound merge. The introspective, reflective, and chamber spirit of this suite emphasizes the vulnerability and the often helpless feelings of attending to those suffering from Alzheimer's when “everything that’s known is gone”, as Wikström sings in the opening piece, “Synker og Stirrerr (Sinking and Staring). “Nelly” captures Filipsen’s father's last memory and gently addresses the realization that when time, with its many memories and experiences, loses its meaning, and all that is left is the present. The power of this thoughtful, insightful suite lies in its emotional restraint, best expressed by Wikström’s fragile voice, and its kaleidoscopic individual colors, suggesting a nuanced yet abruptly shifting, unstable, and not always comprehensible new reality, faithfully representing life with Alzheimer’s disease. But Filipsen orchestrates this suite not as an expression of melancholy and loss, but as a statement of compassion and love to the most closed ones, and the opportunity to let them go, embraced by their dear ones. Or as he wrote in “I stilhed findes ord (In Silence There Are Words): “...Room for honesty, peculiarity, and unbearable sorrow / Come take my hand”. Midt i en Fremtid by The Black Nothing & Anders Filipsen Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Sunnyside Records, 2026 Personnel - Mat Maneri: viola; Lucian Ban: piano; John Hébert: bass; Randy Peterson: drums. Avant-garde violist and composer Mat Maneri is known for blending fragility and crisp friction within a subtly discordant, microtonal approach to music. Mist is the final installment of a trilogy that includes Dust (2019) and Ash (2023), continuing its exploration of heavy, noir-like textures that evoke grief and misery. His quartet features longtime associates: pianist Lucian Ban—who contributes four of the album’s eight compositions—bassist John Hébert, and drummer Randy Peterson. The new album, unrelentingly gloomy, unfolds through a free-flowing discourse, with capriciously oblique gestures creating a sense of erudition and intimate vulnerability. Maneri’s “ Through a Mist Darkly ”, whose title nods to Ingmar Bergman’s emotionally complex drama Through a Glass Darkly —and also recalls the piece of the same name that Maneri recorded on the 1996 album Three Men Walking with his father, saxophonist Joe Maneri, and bassist Joe Morris—is wrapped in a melancholic veil. This pensive, lyrical meditation extends into his shadowy and grief-stricken composition “ Achlys ”, which references the Greek goddess of misery and mist. Here, Maneri injects greater tension and movement into his playing while Ban explores dreamy atmospheres before expanding into imaginative avant-garde flourishes. Ban’s “ A Piece of God ” emanates a grateful serenity, revolving around a recurring thematic phrase over which Maneri’s tearful viola tremolos pierce the heart with quiet forlornness. The pianist also contributes “ Mist ”, an elusive tone poem anchored by Hébert’s spacious bass figure and Peterson’s understated drum colors, and “ Paul Motian ”, an abstract, floating, and exploratory homage to the late drummer, opening with bass and drums alone. Curiously, Maneri—who has long shared an affinity for Motian’s singular musical language—had already included a composition titled “ Motian ” on Dust. Mist takes listeners out of their comfort zone as the quartet glides seamlessly between pitches with remarkable impressionistic finesse. Its main weakness lies in its unwavering devotion to a single atmosphere, offering too little contrast over the course of a slow-burning, 50-minute meditation that demands considerable patience from the listener. Favorite Tracks: 03 - Achlys ► 04 - Mist ► 08 - Missed

items.body:
More than two decades after F4 last performed at Bangkok's IMPACT Arena, three members of the legendary Mandopop group are set to return to the iconic venue for a reunion that many fans have spent years waiting for.

On 1 and 2 August, F✦FOREVER 1st World Tour will arrive at IMPACT Arena, bringing together Jerry Yan, Van Ness Wu, Vic Chou, and Ashin, the lead vocalist of Mayday, for two nights celebrating friendship, nostalgia, and some of Mandopop's most enduring songs.

The Bangkok stop forms part of the group's Southeast Asia run, following an explosive series of concerts across the region. Before heading to Thailand, F✦FOREVER played three consecutive nights at Indonesia Arena, where all 45,000 tickets sold out within seconds. The concerts saw thousands of fans singing along in Mandarin, creating one of the tour's most memorable moments and underscoring the lasting popularity of the project across Southeast Asia.

The regional tour continues with performances in Manila, Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, and Singapore, giving longtime fans throughout the region another opportunity to experience the limited project live.

For Thai audiences, the concerts carry particular emotional weight. F4 became a defining cultural phenomenon across Asia through Meteor Garden, and their music remains closely tied to a generation that grew up with the Taiwanese drama. Returning to the very same venue where F4 performed in August 2004, Jerry Yan, Van Ness Wu, and Vic Chou are set to revisit a chapter that helped shape Asian pop culture, this time joined by Ashin, whose work with Mayday has soundtracked another generation of Mandarin music fans.

Fans can expect a setlist spanning both new material and beloved classics. Signature songs including 'Meteor Rain', 'Can't Lose You', 'Season of Fireworks', and 'The First Time' have all been newly rearranged for the tour, while newer releases such as 'Forever Forever'—a collaboration co-created by Jay Chou and Ashin—and 'Always Be My Bro' will also be performed live.

The production itself is one of the tour's biggest talking points. Backed by an investment of approximately NTD250 million and supported by nearly 300 crew members, the show has been designed as an immersive arena experience.

A specially designed four-point star-shaped stage allows the four performers to move closer to audiences from every direction, while towering crystal-inspired structures, elaborate lighting effects, and expansive visual production transform the venue into what organisers describe as a "City of Stars". Throughout the evening, fans can also expect around 20 different stage outfits showcasing each performer's distinct style.

Beyond the group performances, each member will also take centre stage during dedicated solo segments.

Van Ness Wu is expected to perform material from his latest album Dance Until We Die, bringing his trademark choreography and the viral "Triple Shake" dance phenomenon to the stage.

Vic Chou will revisit favourites including 'The Most Special One' and 'Love in Loving You', alongside newer songs such as 'Who Gave Me the Courage' and 'Tell Me Why'.

Jerry Yan's segment will feature emotional performances of unreleased songs 'Luxury' and 'Insomnia Letter', as well as 'I Really Love You', offering fans a more intimate glimpse into his current musical journey.

Meanwhile, Ashin will perform songs that have become staples of Mayday's catalogue, including 'World Crazy', 'Stubborn', and 'Fool', highlighting the songwriting that has made him one of Mandopop's most celebrated lyricists.

The concert is set to unfold through five thematic chapters—Faith, Friends, Fans, Family, and Fixed Stars—bringing together the group's past and present while celebrating the connection they've built with audiences over the years.

F✦FOREVER itself is a special limited project uniting Jerry Yan, Van Ness Wu, and Vic Chou with Ashin. Since launching, the tour has already completed 19 shows across major Chinese cities including Shanghai, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Wuhan, and Chongqing before expanding into Southeast Asia in response to overwhelming demand.

items.body: The digital gambling landscape in the United Kingdom provides countless chances to enjoy entertainment and win money, but exploring these options requires careful consideration and knowledge. With hundreds of platforms vying for your attention, separating reputable casinos from questionable platforms becomes essential for protecting both your funds and personal information. This comprehensive guide will walk you through the critical factors to assess when selecting a gambling platform, from regulatory compliance and oversight to payment security and customer support, ensuring you choose wisely in your casino experience. Understanding British Online Casino & Licensing The United Kingdom Gambling Commission (UKGC) operates as the primary regulatory authority overseeing all gambling activities within the country, establishing tough regulations that companies need to adhere to to properly deliver offerings to British players. Any service running without a valid UKGC license is conducting illegal business and ought to be bypassed entirely, as these sites lack the user protections and regulation that authorized providers must provide. You can check a casino’s licensing status by looking for the commission’s logo at the bottom of the website and verifying the license number on the UKGC’s official register. Licensed operators must adhere to strict regulatory frameworks covering responsible gambling measures, fair gaming practices, secure financial transactions, and clear disclosure of terms. These requirements include mandatory self-exclusion tools, deposit limits, reality checks, and access to problem gambling support resources, ensuring players have tools to manage over their gaming activities. The UKGC also mandates regular auditing of random number generators and game fairness, separation of customer money from operational accounts, and adherence to strict advertising standards that prohibit targeting vulnerable individuals. Beyond UKGC licensing, trusted operators often hold additional certifications from independent testing agencies such as eCOGRA, iTech Labs, or GLI, which confirm gaming fairness and business standards through regular audits. These third-party seals provide an additional level of assurance that the casino operates transparently and maintains published payout rates for all games. When evaluating potential gambling sites, focus on those showing multiple certifications alongside their UKGC license, as this shows dedication to exceeding minimum regulatory requirements and maintaining top-tier industry practices. Key Safety Features to Consider in UK Online Casinos When reviewing gaming sites, key safety measures function as core markers of a site’s legitimacy and commitment to player protection. These features form the backbone of a trustworthy operation, making certain that your time on the platform stays secure, equitable, and open throughout your interactions with the platform. Knowing which security features matter most allows you to rapidly evaluate any site’s reliability before committing your time and money. The following sections outline the key safety measures that every legitimate UK casino should have as standard. SSL Data Protection and Security Measures Secure Socket Layer (SSL) encryption represents the gold standard for safeguarding personal data sent from your device and the gaming platform’s servers. Look for the padlock icon in your browser’s address bar and verify the URL starts with “https” rather than “http”, indicating that all data exchanges are encrypted using industry-standard protocols. Beyond basic encryption, established platforms implement extensive data protection policies compliant with UK GDPR regulations. These measures include protected storage of personal information, stringent access protocols, and transparent privacy policies that clearly explain how your data is collected, used, and protected throughout your engagement with the operator. Fair Gaming and RNG Certification Random Number Generator (RNG) certification ensures that game outcomes are truly unpredictable and are protected from manipulation by either the operator or players. Third-party testing organizations such as eCOGRA, iTech Labs, and Gaming Laboratories International consistently review these systems, confirming that games run with integrity and payout percentages match stated percentages. Legitimate operators showcase certification seals clearly on their websites, usually in the bottom area, and offer recent audit reports. These certificates verify that games satisfy strict fairness standards and that the platform functions with transparency, giving you confidence that every spin, deal, or roll is decided randomly rather than fixed outcomes. Accountable Gambling Tools and Support Comprehensive gaming responsibility tools demonstrate an operator’s commitment to user safety past mere regulatory compliance. Key features comprise deposit controls, session time notifications, self-exclusion options, and reality check features that assist you in maintain control over your gambling patterns and stop harmful habits from occurring. Premier casino platforms offer links to support organisations including GamCare, BeGambleAware, and Gamblers Anonymous, combined with trained customer support staff who can assist with implementing responsible gaming tools. The availability and accessibility of these resources showcase the operator’s genuine commitment for customer safety and their dedication to promoting safe, sustainable gaming practices. Assessing Payment Security and Financial Methods Payment security serves as a pillar of secure gaming activities, necessitating careful review of encryption standards and payment protections. Trusted casinos implement SSL encryption technology, indicated by the security padlock in your address bar, which shields your financial data during transmission. Look for sites that display trust certificates from established bodies like Thawte or Comodo, and check they use 256-bit or higher encryption standards to ensure your account details stay protected throughout every transaction. The variety and selection of payment options available reflect a platform’s dedication to user safety and ease of use. Trusted operators provide multiple payment options such as credit cards, e-wallets like PayPal and Skrill, direct bank deposits, and prepaid cards such as Paysafecard. Each method should clearly display transaction times, minimum and maximum limits, and any applicable charges. Established platforms partner with reputable payment processors and maintain separate accounts to keep player funds distinct from operational expenses. Withdrawal procedures warrant thorough examination, as this area often exposes a platform’s true reliability and transparency. Reputable platforms establish transparent policies regarding withdrawal timeframes, generally spanning from 24 hours for e-wallets to five business days for wire transfers. Be wary of sites enforcing unreasonable withdrawal limits or requiring excessive documentation beyond standard verification requirements. Check reviews that detail withdrawal experiences, as consistent delays or unexplained holds often indicate problematic practices. Responsible gaming platforms demonstrate their commitment through clear monetary policies and player protection measures. Look for sites that provide spending caps, reality checks, and self-exclusion tools directly within your account settings. The presence of partnerships with organizations like GamCare and BeGambleAware further indicates a platform’s dedication to player welfare. Additionally, review the terms and conditions regarding bonus wagering requirements and cash-out limitations to avoid unexpected complications when accessing your winnings. Reviewing Customer Support and Player Reviews Dependable customer support serves as a cornerstone of reputable gambling platforms, delivering essential assistance when technical issues, transaction inquiries, or account concerns occur. Examining both the speed of customer service and real user testimonials delivers important information into an operator’s commitment to customer satisfaction and equitable service. Assessing Customer Service Quality Before committing funds to any platform, conduct thorough tests of available support channels including live chat, email, and telephone services to evaluate response speed and staff knowledge. Contact support with specific questions about withdrawal procedures, bonus terms, or account verification requirements, noting whether representatives provide clear, accurate information or vague, evasive responses that might indicate operational concerns. Quality gaming platforms generally provide 24/7 multilingual support with experienced staff members who show clear expertise of casino features and compliance standards. Keep track of your support exchanges, noting response times, how useful the answers are, and whether support agents can quickly address queries without unnecessary delays or repeated requests for the same information. Investigating Third-Party User Feedback Review multiple independent review platforms, gaming communities, and consumer protection websites to gather real user feedback rather than relying solely on reviews posted on operator websites. Search for recurring themes in feedback regarding withdrawal processing times, bonus term fairness, game quality, and how disputes are handled by management teams. Exercise care with reviews that appear overly favorable or unusually critical, as both genuine operators and unscrupulous sites may attempt to manipulate public perception through fake testimonials. Focus on detailed reviews from confirmed users that provide specific examples of their experiences, especially concerning financial transactions and support communications during issue handling. Danger Signals and Signs to Avoid When evaluating casino sites, specific red flags should instantly trigger alarm bells about their credibility and security. Be wary of sites that lack clear licensing information, display outdated security certificates, or feature poorly designed websites with many typos and grammar mistakes. Additionally, platforms that pressure you with overly generous promotions that seem too good to be true, or those that render cash-out procedures unnecessarily complicated, often indicate unreliable operators that likely don’t prioritize your best interests at heart. Another critical warning involves online casinos that fail to provide clear terms of service or bury important information in complex legal language meant to mislead players. Be wary of platforms with consistently negative reviews mentioning payment delays, slow support responses, or account closures without adequate justification. Sites that lack established payment options, lack responsible gambling tools, or refuse to verify their gaming integrity through third-party verification should be avoided entirely, as these indicators point to a lack of regulatory compliance. Pay careful attention to how a platform handles your personal data and monetary dealings, as legitimate operators will always emphasize security and transparency. If a casino declines to share clear information about their ownership, presents false regulatory badges, or runs in jurisdictions famous for lax gambling laws, these are critical indicators. Trust your gut feeling—if something feels wrong with a platform’s day-to-day activities, customer interactions, or transaction methods, it’s wise to walk away and choose a more trustworthy alternative that exhibits genuine commitment to customer safety and fair gaming practices.

items.body: Marco Benevento got deep into Italian library-music composers like Alessandro Alessandroni and Piero Umiliani, the people who wrote twenty instrumentals a day for forgotten films, hunting down their records on vinyl and sitting in his car with rare CDs when he couldn’t find them anywhere else. He spent three years in his Woodstock studio writing his own versions of what he heard, and “Big Top” is the result: a Wurlitzer Centura organ, two trumpets and a tuba over a funk groove, with peacock calls and phone voice memos cut into the arrangement. Benevento came up through the New York experimental jazz scene, made three records of purely instrumental music, then took up singing and spent the next decade pulling in every direction at once: psych, rock, Grateful Dead territory with Joe Russo’s Almost Dead, session work for Clairo and Lady Wray. “Big Top” comes from Glera, out on 24 July and his debut for Big Crown Records, a record that drops the vocals and gives the instruments the whole room. He performed “Big Top” live at Diamond Mine, the Long Island City studio co-owned by the Big Crown house band, with Leon Michels on bass, Homer Steinweiss on drums, Scott Metzger on guitar, Dave Guy and Michael Leonhart on trumpets, John Altieri on tuba. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Following their debut album, Io Sono Nato Libero sounds as classic for Banco del Mutuo Soccorso as Selling England by the Pound does for Genesis. In "Canto Nomade Per Un Prigioniero Politico," the piano gives way to the organ, and the composition flows naturally, never flaunting its complexity in a bombastic manner; the dual-keyboard sextet functioned like a small orchestra, expanded here by an additional guitarist and two percussionists. Gianni Nocenzi's piano playing sounds as classically inspired as Tony Banks's, yet turns atonal at will; alongside the organ, the band launches into a free-jazz jam reminiscent of Van der Graaf Generator. One can choose to focus on the piano or Renato D'Angelo's bass, and, despite the improvisational nature of the jam, there is a structured melody that eventually takes on a flamenco flair, until the acoustic guitar is left playing solo, evoking the wild harmonies of Gentle Giant. Flamenco arrives with such staying power that it almost feels like listening to Paco de Luc�a; yet the organ and atonal piano soon return, joined by bass and drums, in a wild, unbridled journey to another dimensi�n, sweeping us along like a whirlwind. It is at the intersection of flamenco and classical music, embodied by Manuel de Falla, that they converge with Banco del Mutuo Soccorso."Non Mi Rompete" is a charming acoustic track with echoes of Emerson, Lake & Palmer; it gives way to the more ambitious "La Citt� Sottile," where the piano moves in unison with the bass and Francesco Di Giacomo's voice seems to rise from the depths of the earth. When a melody is well-written, it shows, in the phrasing and the musicality of the words, transcending the instruments themselves. Marcello Todaro's jazzy electric guitar is a welcome touch, making the track seem to float... until the organ yields to a section featuring classical piano and Minimoog, achieving a unique rhythmic interplay with the vocals, a syncopated drum cadence that carries the melody toward its preordained destination.There is something operatic about Dopo... Niente � Pi� Lo Stesso, something dark, where, following an opening featuring electric guitar and keyboards, we plunge into the void. Francesco Di Giacomo's vocals are a story in themselves; his tenor voice blends seamlessly with the band's music, where the piano takes on the classical hues of Tony Banks, flirting with jazz-rock, before returning to an operatic feel with the sound of the spinet. "Traccia II" is an instrumental track that follows on from the band's debut and closes a magnificent album, simultaneously crowning the band's classic era. Its message, opposing war and championing freedom (a freedom for the masses and the people, not the market), remains more relevant than ever, just like the music itself.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Ezekiel's story is told in this album, which stands as a conceptual work; the entry of the saxophone expanded the jazzier side of the sound, yet the interplay of violin and acoustic guitar brought to mind the third incarnation of Van der Graaf in the late 70s. Juan Carlos P'rez's vocals are warm as ever, and Antton Fernandez's piano work truly displayed virtuosity in the service of the song.These two facets are well represented in "Esnatzea I" and its second part, which features an almost classic-sounding chorus... until the saxophone kicks in. Indeed, Carlos Jimenez's saxophone and Shanti Jimenez's bass drove the rhythm.The boys' choir helps convey Ezekiel's story, even if it doesn't play a major musical role; Itziar Egileor's vocals, on the other hand, truly illuminate "Ikasgaia," evoking Annie Haslam of Renaissance, no small feat. Sung in euskera, it is beautiful, and the second section, with organ, saxophone, and drums hitting exactly where they should, rounds it all out, mirroring the perpendicularity of the tracks depicted on the cover. And the ending with the Rhodes and scat vocals is even crazier, one of the best tracks on the album."Erantzuna" continues the interplay between Rhodes piano, acoustic guitar, and violin, an acoustic nu-jazz-rock sound with a Spanish flavor, and it is that powerful dynamic between the drums and the acoustic guitar that reminded me of Van der Graaf... plus the bass; let us not forget that Nic Potter had returned on bass for The Quiet Zone/The Pleasure Dome.That bohemian spirit present in Spain at the time, the freedom following the dictatorship, the 'Movida Espa'ola', the liberated cinema of early Almod'var and Fernando Colomo, it is all there, in those saxophone notes that so powerfully invite one to dream."Maitasun Kanta Bat" begins with a jazzy interplay between the flute and violin, anchored by the drums; the two instruments weave a delicate ballet that could only be crowned by the electric guitar solo at the end.Jose "Foisis" Garate, the former bassist, was performing his military service, and the band had already split up by the time the album was released. However, the record label had Juan Carlos P'rez release his solo album under the band's name, capitalizing on their previous success.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Norway's PANZERPAPPA is a band that looks to the past but in a much more ambitious manner than mostretro-proggers of recent years. This Oslo musical entity began as far back as 1998 melding theplayful antics of Sweden's Samla Mammas Manna with the darker avant-prog angularities of UniverseZero or Henry Cow all the while adding the warm tones and jazzy textures of England's CanterburyScene. The band's first major lineup up lasted roughly from 1998-2001 when the debut "PasserGullfisk" was released in 2000 and it was evident from the rather amateurish delivery of it all thatthe band hadn't quite reached its primetime. By 2002 the band cemented a more dynamic cast of characters which featured Endre Begby (guitars),Steinar B�rve (saxophones, keys), J�rgen Skjulstad (bass, piano) and Trond Gjellum (drums andpercussion). This new lineup allows the band to blossom into its own brand of avant-jazz-prog andthe first album to appear was HULEMYSTERIET which cryptically means "Cave Mystery" in Norwegian.This release pretty much follows what the debut started but the band feels more confident at thispoint with intricately designed instrumentals that offer varying mood settings that range from themore playful Samlas playbook to the darker pieces of procession prog out of the chamber prog historybooks. Add some stellar saxophone workouts and guitar tones that alternate between clean echoey jazz toagitating rock distortion and what you'll experience is a nice display of PANZERPAPPA taking it allto the next level. With seven mostly lengthy tracks that add up to nearly 49 minutes, the quartet onthis release captures the essence of the 70s Rock In Opposition movement with captivatingperformances that begin with the more swinging opener "Spacefunkopera" to the closing depressive "De99 Trappertrinn" which serves as the album's longest piece at just over 10 minutes. In between thealbum delvers admirable doses of nerdy complex, even labyrinthine compositions that display a knackfor capturing the heavier versions of King Crimson, the more subdued chamber rock nuances of ArtZoyd as well as the whimsical idiosyncrasies of Zappa and the Samlas.The tracks all vary greatly taking different approach with a rathe unpredictable stylistic shiftbetween them but one of the highlights is the eccentric title track with emulates the style ofchildren singing and the breath phases that differentiate them from adults. Add some 19/16 timesignatures and angularity overload fortified with jazz and chamber rock elegance and it easilystands out as the strongest track on the album. Overall this major improvement over the debuthowever it still pales in comparison to the band's next few releases which took things even furtherby making cohesive album experiences. Individually these tracks are all excellent but as an albumthey don't hang together quite as successfully and at this stage the band was still emulating itsheroes without offering that complete original branding. An divine album to experience but not quiteup to the level the next album would hit.3.5 rounded down

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Having heard 'Alice's Eeerie Dream' on Morow some years ago, I finally decided to dig into theentirety of Franck Carducci's debut studio album 'Oddity'. Carducci is a French-born multi-instrumentalist who had moved to Holland at some point, which is where he had met Steve Hackett,among other of his progressive rock heroes, with the French musician himself being a dedicated fanof Floyd, Genesis, and the like. And as the story goes, it was Hackett who had insisted thatCarducci releases an album of all-original material, which is how 2011's 'Oddity' came about. Thisis a very retro-sounding record, showcasing the influence of neo-prog and art rock all the waythrough, with Carducci working out some pastoral symphonic rock soundscapes, while incorporatingflutes and acoustic guitars pretty often, too. At times this record reminisces the old-school SteveHackett LPs, at others it resembles Pendragon way too blatantly, which for me strips away theingenuity of the musical offering.As for the five songs appearing on this record, four of them approach or exceed the ten-minute mark,which is a little tricky given the nature and style of this album. I find some sections in theseextended suites incredibly corny, and while the album has no shortage of excellent instrumentalpassages, too, the overall feel is of something derivative and directionless, which can bothercertain listeners. The opening suite 'Achilles', for example, sitting at fifteen minutes, features amixture of quirky symphonic synths and folk-inspired artsy interludes that just fail to hit thespot. The intimidating length of this composition makes it all the more laborious to go through.Second track 'The Quind' is simply mellow and boring, while 'The Eyes of Age' is a pretty obnoxiouspiece of lousy art rock. The second half of the record brings some retribution, with the 12 minutesof 'Alice's Eerie Dream', which is pretty catchy, rocking, and well-executed, and the closing piece'The Last Oddity', which is mostly instrumental and brings forth some exciting ideas.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The guitars of Matt Stevens and Steve Cleaton feel like stepping into a late-19th-century glass-roofed conservatory, a setting gradually shattered by distortion; as the glass comes crashing down, every note from Kev Feazey's bass makes the floor shake... it is not an earthquake, but "Truck," the opening track of the third album by the English band The Fierce & The Dead, an album titled The Euphoric that heralds a full-color epic.1991 is as fast-paced as punk but as complex as Television or Magazine, bands with whom it shares significant common ground. It offers sonic journeys and layered textures, alongside variations from previous albums, such as the inclusion of technology, which, given the group's progressive leanings, sits perfectly well with their rock-oriented (yet experimental) spirit. Thus, it comes as no surprise that the title track, "The Euphoric," takes on an electro-rock sound, driven by Kev Feazey's programming and synthesizer work."Dancing Robots" is dark, and its use of loops combined with rock-style percussion reminded me of Garbage; yet, when that guitar-fueled pandemonium kicks in, with its abrupt cuts and sustained notes, it evokes Rage Against the Machine. Then comes "Dug Town" to rein in all that energy, encapsulating it within the sound of Bowie's more electronic phase, specifically his collaborations with Fripp, as that cloud of guitars and synths settles back to earth... carrying that ethereal, postmodern modernity that is already turning retro, simply because it has no other choice.That blend of electronica gives "Cadet Opal" an almost symphonic feel, whereas "Verbose" leans toward Garage Glam infused with a good dose of modern psychedelia, that is how one might define it. The track holds many surprises, with dual guitars building a symphony that unfolds like the inner workings of a factory: smokestacks belching fumes while control-panel lights flash with alarm signals, a mix of the classic and the modern."48K" is short, yet it captures the spirit of 90s-era King Crimson combined with classic Black Sabbath. Here, the full-color epic shifts into a blurred black-and-white, yet this is simply another shade that enhances the colors that came before.Parts 7 & 8 bring to a close an album that offered no respite, a peculiar kind of euphoria, perhaps, evoking Portishead yet underpinned by a heavy metal foundation that lends it a gothic edge. Expertly balancing contrasts and subtleties, the track features a coda so soothing and harmonious that it only serves to amplify everything that came before. For The Euphoric is nothing less than a musical metaphor for light.

Were the other artists evenGenesis fans? Or do most Genesis fans have bad taste? Don't answer that. THIS IS TOO GOOD!! Now Ihave reached the second part, no, don't add radio voices!! Don't do the Dream Theather bit, itsucks, it went away as soon as it appeared, now this got serious... but it ends quickly, I wish thefull second part was in here, but I guess they themselves thought that it was too much for thistrash album lol, because the full thing is actually available on one of their albums and itsglorious, highly recommended, in fact, I had already heard this one before, so it is one of the moreknown Cinema Show covers, they even played it live... but talking more about this is beyond thisreview's scope, and this cover is also outside the scope of this album, hence why they cut itprobably.- Broadway Melody of 1974 (Controlled Bleeding): Or Fly In A Windshield really, it sounds ok, not ascool as the original, but it doesn't need to be. After the long improvisation, that was fine,finally at Broadway Melody... this is good, honestly, they changed a bit, it could sound a bitbetter, but there's nothing annoying about it, its just well done and the ending is lovely, I justwish that last part was longer though.- The Waiting Room (Architectual Metaphor): Every cover I have heard of this track is just bad, so Ialready have my hopes low, and ending the album like this I don't think its a good idea, when itstill had so much to prove, having this song at the end tells me that they gave up, that's how badall the covers of this song I have heard are. But this one... it takes a bit to start, but in themiddle it becomes The Waiting Room from the live version, that's a great idea, there are lots ofideas to take from there and to make it in studio, this could be good... but they gave up on that,and decided to get me Aisle Of Plenty'd instead, a good idea if it were well done, now I get whythis is at the end of the album, but it still isn't enough, this is one of the better Waiting RoomsI have heard, but that's not saying much really.Overall, this album was not very good, there are pieces that feel incomplete, others that actuallyare and were meant to be that way, others that just don't work at all, but there's good in here too,maybe this album could inspire others to do better, but as it stands, in this internet age wereevery cover can be found, and knowing that there were better tribute albums released before, I justfind hard to believe that people were so good towards this album, was it because of the names? Arethey really ok with the mixing on this one? Was this really that good in the context of that year?In any case, nowadays it is not, I would give it 2 stars easily, but I'm going to give it 1, just tolower the very high ranking, I'm sorry.

items.body: Review by trickert — This is an underrated album, on many levels. Let's start first with concept. Julian Cope remarks in his classic Krautrocksampler book that Individuellos took La Dusseldorf's "funny Bavarian sound to its logical conclusion." Cope never lacks for insight, of course, but here he oddly stops short. His framing narrative for what we call krautrock is that young German teens were aghast at what their parents and Germany had done, and sought musical exploration and escape based on rock and avant garde models. What Cope I think does not see is that this album is complete reimagination through music of what Bavarian-based Germany was and could be. That's why it uses the Bavarian sounds. It is completely reworking them, turning them away from their past towards a present and future that the band could live in, could build on, could dream out of. Once you hear this, you hear how the Bavarian sounds are not funny. They are a possibility. Overall, this album continues the La Dusseldorf sound of motorik beats, simple and melodic vocals, and an upbeat vibe, with an always present moodiness that is difficult to describe. The two exceptions are two ambient tracks that mix Bavarian feels and sound effects, one on each side, but I think that these cement the concept without overstaying their welcome: they are musical re-imaginations of the Bavarian soundscape. Overall, the album fundamentally re-imagines what Germany was or could be from the musical ground up, and it is an absolutely brilliant statement, because the concept never takes over from the accessibility of the music. A five star classic.

items.body: Review by trickert — I'm a little surprised at seeing some of the middling reviews some people have of this album. It's a much better album than that. That it's more pastoral and melodic in places seems to be a strike against it for some. I guess, if you expect the rougher, more proto-punk aspects Neu! again. But Neu! were experimental and spotty--the great stuff was generational, of course, but there were middling tracks throughout, especially on Neu! 2. Those who have listened to the first Harmonia album know it is an exercise in experimental tension. If you expect that here, you will be disappointed. If you are open to this band trying new things in a more melodic vein, then this is a great leap forward. Side 1 has cool motorik beats and smoother Neu!-ish instrumental and vocal approach, a bit more song-oriented, but certainly not pop. Side 2 is more overtly instrumental, forecasting the subdued and minimalist albums Moebius and Roedelius would do in the late 70s and 80s. Overall, this is simply essential. It is the blueprint for La Dusseldorf, and might be thought of as their first album, in essence. Then go get all three La Dusseldorf albums, which are amazing albums, and never duplicated.

items.body: Zu meinen Lieblingsalben aller Zeiten gehört Remain in Light von Talking Heads. Seinen fragmentierten Charakter bezieht das Album vor allem daraus, dass sich die Band hier gewissermaßen selbst gesamplet hat: Akribisch erarbeitete Loops wurden in einen organisch wirkenden Bandkontext überführt. Alles live – und doch irgendwie nicht. Zu meinen Lieblingsalben der bisherigen 2020er-Jahre gehört Girl with Fish von Feeble Little Horse. Darauf bedient die junge Indie-Band aus Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, mit ihrem glitchigen Shoegaze-Pop eines meiner liebsten Subgenres: ultraeingängige Rockmusik, die permanent so klingt, als würde sie auseinanderfallen. Zu meinen Lieblingsalben des Jahres 2026 gehört Bitknot, ebenfalls von Feeble Little Horse. Hier werden die grundlegenden Ästhetiken von Remain in Light und Girl with Fish gewissermaßen miteinander verschmolzen. Wie schon das vorherige Explosivwerk der Band ist auch Bitknot kurz, knackig und geprägt von ultradröhnenden Gitarrenakkorden sowie der nüchtern-süßen Stimme von Frontfrau Lydia Slocum. Darüber hinaus verfolgt die Gruppe einen Ansatz, der an die Talking Heads zur Zeit von Remain in Light erinnert: Es klingt, als würden eingespielte Aufnahmen digital bearbeitet, zerhackt und wieder zusammengesetzt – scheinbar willkürlich, tatsächlich aber mit Präzision. Die Digital Audio Workstation wirkt dabei wie ein weiteres Bandmitglied. Allzu weit wird dieses Prinzip jedoch nicht getrieben; im Kern bleiben die Stücke eingängige Popsongs mit Rockfundament. Ein digitales, zugängliches Sample- und Gitarrengewitter.

items.body: Vergessen wir kurz Ibiza, vergessen wir die kalkulierte Sonnenabstraktion, mit der Muriel Grossmann sonst den Balearenjetset aus der Fassung schraubt. Hier brennt das nackte Jetzt im Nacken. Und zwar mit einem Gruß aus der Vergangenheit: Tallinn, Spätherbst 2025, draußen klirrt das Nichts, drinnen ein vollkommen freies Studiogefecht mit dem estnischen Großjazzer Tõnu Naissoo. Wo jüngere Alben von Muriel wie Light of Mind oder Breakthrough noch kontemplativ klotzten, läuft das hier so: Grossmann peitscht ihr Saxofon und die Flöte durch schimmernde Modalwellen, während Naissoo an der heiligen Dreifaltigkeit aus Orgel, Rhodes und Moog kosmische Breitwandhypnosen ausrollt. Natürlich gibt es da keine Ausreden, keinen doppelten Boden, nicht mal ein Sicherheitsnetz rollt die Packungsbeilage von NooPop Records aus. Nur diesen sauguten Echtzeitexzess, der sich niederkniet vor Coltrane, Shorter und wie sie alle geheißen haben.

items.body: For over three decades, Culture Kultür has been a well-established name on the international Future-Pop and Synth-Pop scene. Since its formation in 1992, the Spanish duo – comprising Josua and vocalist Salva Maine—has built a strong reputation for crafting danceable, melodic Electronic music with a strong emphasis on meaningful themes and lyrics. Over the years, the band has produced several hit songs, many of which were revisited last year on the compilation album “Time”, featuring newly reworked versions of their best-known songs. With the release of “Atomic” on Caustic Records, the duo opens an exciting new chapter. The album combines their signature Future-Pop sound with a contemporary production, exploring themes such as human connection, technological alienation, and the uncertainties of modern life. The result is an impressive collection of songs that may well represent their strongest work to date. The release of “Atomic” provides the perfect opportunity to look back on more than three decades of music with Culture Kultür, while also exploring the inspiration, creative process, and stories behind this remarkable new album. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Culture Kultür interview Q: With Culture Kultür, you can already look back on a long and rich career. What does a new album like “Atomic” represent for you in the context of your extensive discography, and how would you summarize and describe this album yourselves? Josua: You are right. 34 years have passed already since our first 12’ release. Almost a whole life. I must say “Atomic” is in some ways, a different beast to our previous releases. The 10 tracks of the album have been in various processes of completion since the 2020 pandemic. The release of the compilation album “Time” stopped a little the continuation of new songs but as soon as it was released, Salva and I resumed work and I must say releasing “Time” fueled even more the desire to have the new material which was waiting to be fully finished. As every time I close an album, now with the record in my hands, the feeling is ‘how am I going to surpass this one’? I hope this sentiment will be overcome soon. This album comprises our true evolution on composing, Salva vocal performance advance and detailed sound design. I should say it is our best yet. Salva: For me, this is one of our strongest albums, if not the strongest. In fact I think we will play it in full at our next shows in Germany, which we have never done before. Also, it has been one of our fastest works. Apart from the initial songwriting, it only took us six months to finish the songs, record the vocals, and complete the mixing. Q: “Atomic” is the title of the new Culture Kultür album, but it is also a powerful word that can be associated with science and progress on the one hand, and unfortunately with destruction and impermanence on the other. What does this word signify as the title of your album, and what ideas or concepts lie behind it? Josua: Absolutely. Since the very beginning we wanted the title “Atomic” for the album. As a child of the XXth Century, I’m totally fascinated by the atomic energy destined to save us all under its infinite almost free energy for everyone and also the impending doom waiting to happen in an unstoppable nuclear war ready to destroy us all. Atomic energy is the two sides of the future and also our album lyrics reflect deep emotions and hopes, profound fears and wishes. Salva: The initial idea, at least for the design, was to lean toward the darker side of the atomic concept. But later we shifted toward the concept of energy, of the hidden elements that we cannot see but that build everything. Q: Technology seems to be a recurring theme in your work in several ways. As human beings and as musicians, what is your relationship with technology and its rapid advancement? Looking at the situation today, do you think technology has brought people closer together or driven them further apart? And which human and artistic qualities do you believe can never be replaced by machines? Salva: The problem with technology is that it develops faster than our minds can cope with. I once read that we consume as much information in a single day as a person in the Middle Ages would have consumed in an entire lifetime. We are hyperconnected, yet at the same time many of us are afraid to call a friend and instead prefer to send a text message. Technology also enables us to work and live at a pace that our minds cannot sustain for long, so it is no wonder that mental health issues are so common these days. But I think that, in general, it has enabled more connections than separations. I don’t know if, in the future, all our human characteristics can be replicated, but we are not at that point yet. Josua: In our CD release “Manifesto” (year 1999), our phrase for it and also in the back cover was ‘save the technology’. I still believe that. Technology MUST be saved for mankind to use freely and use as a way to expand ourselves as creative and sentient souls. Tech helped me to develop a musical career and also being able to paint the music inside me on the canvas of life. Sadly, the same tech is also creating the destruction of nature and some human relations. Is this a tech fault or it is just ourselves? These are questions difficult to answer. Do we have the responses?… no .. I only have more questions while I look to the coming horizon waiting for better things to happen. Q: What were the biggest challenges during the creation of this album? Did you notice any conscious or unconscious evolution in your creative process compared to previous releases? Josua: The global pandemic was without doubt a ‘turning point’ for some and also for me. Now that terrible event seems almost forgotten and life is now again ‘business as usual’. Not a single lesson has been learned and we go walking again in a straight line to the cliff like Hamelin rats following the music politicians and warmongers are playing. For me, losing friends and relatives was something with a big impact and started a fire inside to again compose songs for me, and if possible, for the world. Regarding the new approach to composing, there was an important change and it was to concentrate on ‘melody first’. And also ‘story / lyrics first’. Rhythm, mood or arrangement are just second priorities. Some of the tracks were totally wrapped around a story to be told, a message to deliver or the main chord structure and melodies. In the past, maybe rhythm was too important to define the tracks. Now for me it is not… the rhythm serves the purpose of the song. Q: I would still describe the Culture Kultür music as ‘Future-Pop’, a term and style that nowadays mainly evokes a sense of nostalgia and is explored by relatively few artists. How do you view that label, and how important is it for you to be associated with a specific genre or niche, particularly from a promotional perspective? Salva: The label is supposed to represent elements of Synth-Pop, EBM, and Trance, so I’m fully on board with it. We never thought about changing the style of our music because of its popularity. We simply did what we wanted to do with the musical elements we love. Josua: Personally, I don’t have a problem with that ‘label’ or ‘style’ name. The truth is we walked along some different styles along our musical journey and if someone wants to ‘tag’ our music as Future-Pop… absolutely no problem for me. On the other hand there have been wonderful bands and songs born under that style and rejecting a sound heritage so powerful and deep because it is ‘dated’ makes no sense. Let’s embrace the music which just makes us feel and ‘move us’ inside out and let’s forget oppressing ‘labeling’. Q: I noticed that “Atomic” reached No. 1 in the DAC (Deutsche Alternative Charts). What does this achievement mean to you as a band, especially in a country with an important scene like Germany? What impact do you expect it to have in terms of album sales, live performances, and other opportunities? Josua: Yes, that was great news and I cannot be more grateful to all the people, critics, fans; comments and excellent album reception in general. Germany has always been ‘second home’ for us and truly playing live in the past has been a blast!! This album has a song in German for the first time ever. This was as a compliment for so many fans in Germany and the always warm welcome we receive there. Absolutely looking forward to playing live soon wherever we are requested. Nothing could be better than to take “Atomic” to the live stage and share the moment with the fans. Salva: We’ve seen a lot of positive reactions: apart from the DAC and GEWC charts, many radio stations and podcasts have shared different songs from the album. We’ve seen an increase in streaming, and there has also been more interest in the physical editions. So our intention is to be able to present the album properly in Germany. Q: Last year, Culture Kultür released “Time”, an album featuring a selection of reworked older songs. How do you look back on your past achievements and the path the band has taken so far? And what are your expectations and ambitions for the future? Salva: I think we have a bunch of good songs and, more importantly, songs that have left a mark on some people’s lives. Our songs have also allowed us to get to know many interesting people, places, and scenes. I think that’s the main thing for us: to enjoy making music that connects with other people. My only ambition is to continue enjoying creating music and sharing it with the world. Josua. Working in older songs was at the same time rewarding and sad. First, you take your old sounds and try to make them new, better, bolder, but also don’t want to betray that ‘old you’ who did the track. The memory lane works both ways, so you remember that ‘yourself’ who did the song at that time… your dreams then… your worries which now seem so small… and people who were around and enjoyed that music which now are not with us… On the very positive side, it was very good to face again some tracks which some fans know how to sing word by word and give them respect and new approach. When the album “Time” was completed, a new view of our musical career arose in front of me and even knowing we had long silent spaces in between albums, a real path of creation was clear to be seen. The future is always an unknown country but I’m sure after several concerts we are now scheduling, we will resume work soon as some tracks are already requesting to be finished and who am I to refuse music’s call ?

items.body: IKON, the Melbourne darkwave, post-punk and gothic rock band, released the single “The Witness Tree” on 4 July 2026. The two-track single previews a forthcoming compilation, “Collective Illusion: The Singles 1998-2026”, which gathers 32 non-album singles and exclusive renditions from across 28 years. IKON has not announced a release date for the compilation. The Witness Tree single by IKON Inside IKON’s ‘The Witness Tree’ single “The Witness Tree” pairs the title track with “My Black Mirror”, both listed as 7-inch single versions, and is available on Bandcamp. IKON recorded the single at Shrimp Shack Studios in Melbourne between 2024 and 2026. Michael Hubbard engineered the session, Chris McCarter and Michael Hubbard produced it, and Adam Calaitzis mixed it at Toyland Studios. Lucie Zann created the artwork. “Collective Illusion: The Singles 1998-2026” collects 32 non-album singles and exclusive renditions, with “The Witness Tree” issued ahead of it. The set continues a run of retrospective releases from the band. In 2023 IKON compiled its early years on “The Complete Recordings 1992-1996”, a four-CD box set on Cleopatra Records, and in March 2026 the label returned to the catalogue with the “Resonance – An Anthology 1998-2009” box set. A 2020 collection, “The Thirteenth Hour: The Singles 2007-2020”, had already drawn together a later stretch of the band’s singles. About IKON Chris McCarter (vocals, guitar, programming) and Dino Molinaro (bass) began writing songs as high-school students in Melbourne in 1988. The pair first worked under the name Death in the Dark, then changed it to IKON in 1991. Original singer Michael Carrodus fronted the band’s first two albums, “In the Shadow of the Angel” (1994) and “Flowers for the Gathering” (1996), which reached goth audiences in Europe and the United States through releases on Apollyon and Metropolis Records. Carrodus left in 1997, and McCarter took over vocals. “This Quiet Earth” (1998) shifted toward electronic composition and produced the singles “Subversion” and “Ghost in My Head”, while “On the Edge of Forever” (2001) returned to the band’s rock sound and brought IKON back to live performance. The group toured Europe for the first time in August 2001, played M’era Luna in 2002 and made its first appearance at Wave-Gotik-Treffen in 2003. The “Psychic Vampire” EP (2004) was followed by the albums “Destroying the World to Save It” (2005) and “Love, Hate and Sorrow” (2009). Later albums include “Everyone Everything Everywhere Ends” (2014) and “Realm of the Black Sun” (2024). Alongside the studio records, IKON’s back catalogue has been reissued and compiled steadily, from Cleopatra’s box sets to a run of double-CD reissues. McCarter also works outside the band: he issued the solo EP “Atmosphere” in 2024, and former members carried IKON’s post-punk sound into the side project Chiron. “The Witness Tree” and the coming “Collective Illusion” compilation extend that singles history into 2026.

items.body: A Tomb Full of Stars “1: When the Reflection Passes” is the debut album from the American experimental duo A Tomb Full of Stars, set for release on September 22, 2026. The five-track “1: When the Reflection Passes” is the first full-length from R. Hunter and Sean Victory, with the lead single “Beneath Bruised Sea” arriving on July 17, 2026. 1: When the Reflection Passes by A Tomb Full of Stars A Tomb Full of Stars build tracks from synthesizers, electronics, percussion, processed voice and field recordings, with layers that accumulate and then recede across passages of harmony, distortion and silence. The duo describes the project as emerging from a shared instinct: “a shared pull toward texture, atmosphere, and the emotional weight that lives beneath noise.” A Tomb Full of Stars detail ‘1: When the Reflection Passes’ The album runs five tracks: “Beneath Bruised Sea”, “We Can See Forever”, “Veiled Levity”, “The Battered Angels of Our Nature” and “Repose”. The opening single combines rolling percussion, low frequencies and suspended melodic figures; “We Can See Forever” moves glitched drones and processed vocals through wider harmonic shifts; “Repose” closes the record on sustained synthesis and sparse melody. The duo assembled the pieces from extended improvisations, then edited them down, treating the voice as another instrument that moves between clear lines and abstraction. “1: When the Reflection Passes” was recorded in Chicago, Illinois and Vancouver, Washington, and mastered by James Plotkin at Plotkinworks. Artwork is by Saprophial, with the band logo by Lucas Allen Cook and layout and design by Sjøli Design. The album and its lead single are available through Bandcamp. About A Tomb Full of Stars A Tomb Full of Stars is an American dark ambient and experimental duo formed by R. Hunter and Sean Victory, working between Chicago, Illinois and Vancouver, Washington. Both had recorded on their own for years before starting the project together. “1: When the Reflection Passes”, set for September 22, 2026, is their first full-length as a duo, preceded by the single “Beneath Bruised Sea” on July 17, 2026. The record was mastered by James Plotkin at Plotkinworks, a studio known for work across experimental, drone and metal.

items.body: CallSubLoop() “Flesh & Resonance” is the debut EP from the coldwave and darkwave project CallSubLoop(), self-released on Bandcamp on July 11, 2026. The three-track “Flesh & Resonance” mixes coldwave, darkwave and acid techno. Flesh & Resonance by CallSubLoop() CallSubLoop() bring a sound that mixes coldwave and darkwave textures with acid-techno rhythms. The EP runs as a three-part sequence: “Trapped in the rhythm of the midnight pulse”, “Built to hold you” and “Flesh, Rendered”. CallSubLoop() ‘Flesh & Resonance’: a three-track concept CallSubLoop() describes the EP as a single narrative told from shifting perspectives. The opening track takes the point of view of a dancer held by the rhythm that drives him; the second moves to the machine that produces the sound and begins to register something it was not built to feel; the closing track brings the two together, the dancer to the beat that keeps him upright and the machine to the sound it makes best. “Flesh & Resonance” is available to stream and buy on Bandcamp. About CallSubLoop() CallSubLoop() is a coldwave, darkwave and acid-techno project. “Flesh & Resonance”, issued on July 11, 2026, is its debut release, self-released digitally through Bandcamp. The three tracks mark the project’s first published material; no earlier releases, label or lineup details have been made public.
